about.title: Rancho Cucamonga Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Getting hurt at work in Rancho Cucamonga usually starts a workers' compensation claim, and for many people that is where it ends. California law makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault. What often goes unnoticed is the second question: did someone other than your employer contribute to the injury? A subcontractor on a job site, a property owner who ignored a hazard, a company that built faulty equipment, or another driver on I-15 or SR-210 while you were making a work run can each be responsible in a separate claim. Those third-party claims carry a two-year deadline and can cover losses workers' comp does not. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect injured workers in San Bernardino County with an independent attorney who looks at both sides of the picture. The attorneys in our network handle cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. Report the injury to your employer within 30 days, then let someone review whether a second path applies to you.

items.title: We look past the workers' comp ceiling
items.desc: Workers' comp is generally your only remedy against your employer, but it does not cover everything. An independent attorney can check whether a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or driver opens a separate claim.

items.title: Deadlines are tracked from day one
items.desc: You have 30 days to report the injury to your employer, and any third-party claim in California carries a two-year deadline. The attorney you are matched with helps keep both clocks in view.

items.title: Retaliation is illegal, and you are not alone
items.desc: California law prohibits an employer from punishing you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If that happens, the attorney can address it alongside your injury case, with no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hit on Foothill Boulevard while driving for work. Is that just a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. If you were on the clock, workers' comp should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, which follows California's two-year deadline. Rancho Cucamonga recorded 474 injury collisions in 2025, with reports peaking on Fridays between 5 and 7 p.m., so work-related crashes on Foothill Boulevard, I-15, and SR-210 are not unusual.

items.question: Do I have to report my injury right away?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days. Reporting sooner is better, because it starts your workers' comp claim and creates a record of what happened. Your employer cannot legally retaliate against you for reporting.

items.question: Can I sue my employer if the injury was their fault?
items.answer: In most cases, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer in California, even when the employer was careless. The separate claim comes into play when a third party, such as a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker, shares responsibility. An independent attorney can tell you whether that applies to your situation.
